title: 07. Google ADK: Day 8 — Session Services — InMemory, Database & VertexAi
summary: Pick the right backend for your state — and survive restarts, scale, and concurrency
objectives: Visual — Three session services side by side

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Pick the right backend for your state — and survive restarts, scale, and concurrency

Day 8 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Memorize the `BaseSessionService` contract: `create_session`, `get_session`, `list_sessions`, `delete_session`, `append_event`, `get_user_state`, `flush`

- Choose between `InMemorySessionService`, `DatabaseSessionService`, and `VertexAiSessionService` based on persistence, scale, and ops requirements

- Configure `DatabaseSessionService` with the three supported async drivers (SQLite, Postgres, MySQL) and migrate schemas with `adk migrate session`

- Use `VertexAiSessionService` with the `agentengine://` URI scheme on Google Cloud Agent Runtime

- Handle `SessionNotFoundError` with `Runner(..., auto_create_session=True)` and use `_sync` variants in non-async contexts

sections.title: 1. Why this matters
sections.body:
An agent's intelligence lives in the LLM, but its *memory* — what the user said, what tools were called, what state was set — lives in the session service. Pick the wrong one and you ship one of two failures: either your agent forgets everything when the container restarts (InMemory in production), or you spend two weeks fighting Postgres connection pool exhaustion because no one told you ADK requires async drivers.

The session service is the most consequential infrastructure decision in an ADK deployment. It dictates whether state survives restarts (yes for Database/Vertex, no for InMemory), whether you can scale horizontally (yes for Vertex/Databases, no for InMemory), whether you can read user state without an active session (yes for InMemory/Database, no for VertexAi), and what your cloud bill looks like. Get it wrong and you are looking at a migration — which is non-trivial because the three services have *different* concurrency models, *different* URI schemes, and *different* feature support.

Today we will walk through all three implementations with working code, internalize the abstract `BaseSessionService` contract they all share, and learn the operational details that bite in production: the async-driver requirement for DatabaseSessionService, the `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row-level locking on Postgres/MySQL, the v1.22.0 schema migration that requires `adk migrate session`, the `SessionNotFoundError` exception that `auto_create_session=True` papers over, and the `_sync` variants you call from synchronous code paths. By the end you will be able to design a session strategy for any deployment topology.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts
sections.body:
Five building blocks: the abstract API, the three implementations, URI schemes, the `_sync` variants, and the `SessionNotFoundError` problem.

### 2.1 The `BaseSessionService` contract

Every session service — InMemory, Database, VertexAi, or your own custom subclass — implements the same seven methods. Internalize this signature; everything else is implementation detail.

```python
from google.adk.sessions import BaseSessionService

class BaseSessionService(abc.ABC):
    async def create_session(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, state: dict | None = None,
        session_id: str | None = None,
    ) -> Session: ...

    async def get_session(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, session_id: str,
    ) -> Session: ...

    async def list_sessions(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str,
    ) -> ListSessionsResponse: ...

    async def delete_session(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, session_id: str,
    ) -> None: ...

    async def append_event(self, session: Session, event: Event) -> Event: ...

    async def get_user_state(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str,
    ) -> State: ...

    async def flush(self) -> None: ...
```

A few things worth noticing:

- **`create_session` accepts an optional `session_id`** — supply your own (e.g. an external correlation ID) and ADK uses it verbatim. Omit it and ADK generates a UUID4.
- **`create_session` accepts an optional `state` dict** — initial state. Great for seeding config on first-run.
- **`append_event` takes a `Session` not IDs** — you pass the live `Session` object; the service looks up its IDs internally. This is why mutating `session.state` directly is unsafe (Day 07): `append_event` reads the deltas tracked through `EventActions.state_delta`, not the snapshot you are holding.
- **`flush()` is a hint, not a guarantee** — DatabaseSessionService uses it to commit pending writes; InMemorySessionService is a no-op; VertexAiSessionService flushes its internal buffer to the runtime.
- **`get_user_state` is optional in practice** — `VertexAiSessionService` raises `NotImplementedError`. If you call it on a service you do not control (e.g. a custom service loaded from a plugin), wrap it in `try/except NotImplementedError`.

### 2.2 InMemorySessionService — dev / unit tests only

The default. Pure Python dicts in process memory; no I/O, no setup, no persistence. Every `Session`, every `Event`, every `user:` and `app:` state value lives in a Python dict keyed by `(app_name, user_id, session_id)`.

```python
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService

svc = InMemorySessionService()
session = await svc.create_session(
    app_name="my_app",
    user_id="alice",
    state={"session:initial_topic": "onboarding"},  # optional seed
)
```

Strengths: zero config, zero latency, zero dependencies. Perfect for unit tests, `adk run` prototyping, and Jupyter notebooks (like this one).

Weaknesses: **state evaporates on process restart**. If you deploy with InMemory in production, every container restart wipes all user conversations. Horizontal scaling is impossible — two replicas have independent dicts. There is no concurrency control beyond a single in-process lock, so do not run it under heavy load.

The `_sync` variants (`create_session_sync`, `get_session_sync`, `delete_session_sync`, `list_sessions_sync`) are particularly useful with InMemory, because they let you write synchronous code without `asyncio.run(...)` noise. They are implemented as thin wrappers around `asyncio.run(self.create_session(...))`.

```
SESSION LIFECYCLE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. create_session(app_name, user_id, state?, session_id?)   │
  │    → returns Session with a fresh id (or your custom id)    │
  │    → initial state optional (good for seeded config)        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 2. runner.run_async(user_id, session_id, new_message)       │
  │    Runner fetches session, passes state+history to agent    │
  │    Each yielded Event triggers append_event internally      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 3. append_event(session, event)  ← you rarely call this    │
  │    Persists the event; applies state_delta / artifact_delta │
  │    Updates session.last_update_time                          │
  │    Concurrency: in-process lock + SELECT...FOR UPDATE (DB)  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 4. get_session(session_id)  ← re-fetch after a pause       │
  │    list_sessions(app_name, user_id)  ← enumerate            │
  │    get_user_state(app_name, user_id)  ← read user scope     │
  │      (raises NotImplementedError on VertexAiSessionService)  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 5. delete_session(session_id)  ← cleanup / GDPR / logout   │
  │    flush()  ← force-write any buffered state (Database)     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### 2.3 DatabaseSessionService — persistent, self-hosted

When you need state to survive restarts but do not want to depend on Google Cloud, use `DatabaseSessionService`. It supports three backends via SQLAlchemy async drivers:

| Backend | Driver string | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SQLite | `sqlite+aiosqlite://` | Local file. Great for single-host deployments. No network latency. |
| PostgreSQL | `postgresql+asyncpg://` | Recommended for production. Row-level locking works. |
| MySQL / MariaDB | `mysql+aiomysql://` | Also supported. Row-level locking works. |

**The async driver is mandatory.** Sync drivers (`sqlite://`, `postgresql://`) will fail at runtime because ADK's entire I/O layer is async. Install with `pip install google-adk[db]` — this pulls `aiosqlite`, `asyncpg`, and `aiomysql` plus SQLAlchemy 2.x.

```python
from google.adk.sessions import DatabaseSessionService

# SQLite (single file) — best for dev / single-host prod
svc = DatabaseSessionService(db_url="sqlite+aiosqlite:///./adk_sessions.db")

# Postgres (production) — connection pool, row-level locking
svc = DatabaseSessionService(
    db_url="postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@db.internal:5432/adk"
)
```

**Concurrency model**: every `append_event` call is wrapped in a two-layer lock. Layer 1 is an in-process `asyncio.Lock` per session (prevents two coroutines in the same process from racing). Layer 2 is a database `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the session row (prevents two *processes* from racing). SQLite supports layer 2 via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, though in practice you should not run SQLite in multi-process deployments.

**Schema migration**: the database schema changed in ADK v1.22.0 (added columns for new event fields). If you have an existing database from an older ADK version, run `adk migrate session <db_url>` once before upgrading. New databases are created with the current schema automatically — no migration needed.

**The `flush()` call**: DatabaseSessionService buffers writes in a transaction. `await svc.flush()` forces a commit. Useful in tests where you want to assert state immediately, or before a clean shutdown.

⚠️ Important

**Common prod gotcha**: forgetting to run `adk migrate session` after upgrading ADK across the v1.22.0 boundary. Symptoms are cryptic — usually a `column "..." does not exist` error on the first `append_event` call. Always run the migration in your deploy script: `adk migrate session "$DATABASE_URL" && exec adk api_server ...`

### 2.4 VertexAiSessionService — managed on Google Cloud

For deployments on Google Cloud's Agent Runtime (Agent Engine), use `VertexAiSessionService`. State is stored in Google-managed infrastructure, scales globally, and integrates with the rest of Vertex AI (evals, monitoring, model garden).

```python
from google.adk.sessions import VertexAiSessionService

svc = VertexAiSessionService(
    project="my-gcp-project",
    location="us-central1",
)

# app_name must be the Reasoning Engine ID or full resource name:
#   "projects/my-gcp-project/locations/us-central1/reasoningEngines/1234567890"
session = await svc.create_session(
    app_name="projects/my-gcp-project/locations/us-central1/reasoningEngines/1234567890",
    user_id="alice",
)
```

Install with `pip install google-adk[gcp]`. Authentication uses Application Default Credentials (ADC) — set up with `gcloud auth application-default login` locally, or via the service account attached to your Cloud Run / GKE workload in production.

**URI scheme for `adk` CLI flags**: when you start `adk web`, `adk run`, or `adk api_server` with `--session_service_uri`, you can pass `agentengine://<reasoning_engine_id>` and ADK will construct the `VertexAiSessionService` for you. Similarly, `memory://` selects `InMemorySessionService` and any SQLAlchemy URL selects `DatabaseSessionService`.

**Two important limitations**: `get_user_state()` raises `NotImplementedError` on VertexAi — to read user state, enumerate `list_sessions(app_name, user_id)` and merge their state dicts. And you cannot use a `VertexAiSessionService` against a local `adk run` session without first deploying your agent to Agent Engine — see Day 14 for the deployment workflow.

```
THREE SESSION SERVICES — PICK ONE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                 InMemory          Database              VertexAi
                 ─────────         ─────────             ────────
  persistence    process memory    SQLite / PG / MySQL   Google Cloud
  restart        ✗ all lost        ✓ survives            ✓ survives
  scale          1 process         1 DB cluster          global
  install        built-in          google-adk[db]        google-adk[gcp]
  URI scheme     memory://         sqlite+aiosqlite://…  agentengine://…
                                       postgresql+asyncpg://…
                                       mysql+aiomysql://…
  concurrency    in-process lock   lock + SELECT FOR UPD  managed
  cost           $0                DB hosting $$         GCP per-call $$
  get_user_state ✓                 ✓                     ✗ NotImplemented
  use case       dev / unit test   self-hosted prod      GCP-managed prod
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### 2.5 `_sync` variants and `SessionNotFoundError`

**Sync wrappers.** Every async method on `BaseSessionService` has a `_sync` sibling: `create_session_sync`, `get_session_sync`, `list_sessions_sync`, `delete_session_sync`, `append_event_sync`, `get_user_state_sync`, `flush_sync`. They are implemented as `asyncio.run(self.X(...))` and exist for code paths that cannot be async — Django views, synchronous Celery tasks, simple scripts. They are *not* a free pass to write your whole app synchronously: each call spins up a fresh event loop, which is wasteful in hot paths.

```python
# Synchronous path — useful in scripts and sync frameworks
session = svc.create_session_sync(app_name="my_app", user_id="alice")
sessions = svc.list_sessions_sync(app_name="my_app", user_id="alice")
```

**`SessionNotFoundError`.** Raised by `get_session` (and by the Runner internally) when the requested `session_id` does not exist. In a typical web app, this happens when a user's session expired, was deleted by a cleanup job, or the user is hitting a stale URL.

Two ways to handle it. The clean way is `try/except`:

```python
from google.adk.sessions import SessionNotFoundError

try:
    session = await svc.get_session(
        app_name="my_app", user_id=user_id, session_id=session_id,
    )
except SessionNotFoundError:
    session = await svc.create_session(app_name="my_app", user_id=user_id)
```

The convenient way is `Runner(..., auto_create_session=True)`:

```python
runner = Runner(
    agent=root_agent,
    app_name="my_app",
    session_service=svc,
    auto_create_session=True,  # ← creates a new session if missing
)
```

With `auto_create_session=True`, the Runner catches `SessionNotFoundError` internally, creates a fresh session, and proceeds. This is the right default for chat backends where you do not want to pepper your code with try/except blocks. The trade-off: a stale `session_id` silently creates a new session, which can confuse users who think they are continuing an old conversation.

🚀 Pro Tip

`InMemoryRunner` (a thin subclass of `Runner`) bundles `InMemorySessionService` for you — no need to construct the service explicitly. Use it for quick scripts: `runner = InMemoryRunner(agent=root_agent, app_name="demo")`. State is lost when the runner is garbage-collected, which is usually what you want for one-off demos.

sections.title: 5. Visual — Three session services side by side
sections.body:
The pre-generated matplotlib diagram shows the three implementations and their key trade-offs. Use it as a cheat sheet when designing a new deployment.

```python
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename="images/day08_session_services.png"))
```

💡 Key Concept

The URI scheme line at the top of the diagram is your single source of truth for `--session_service_uri` flags on the CLI. `memory://` → InMemory, `sqlite+aiosqlite://` / `postgresql+asyncpg://` / `mysql+aiomysql://` → Database, `agentengine://` → VertexAi. Same flag, three backends — pick by changing the URI string.

sections.title: 6. Four Progressive Examples
sections.body:
Today's examples walk through each service, then show multi-user session management. By Example 4 you will have the patterns for a multi-tenant production deployment.

1. **Example 1** — InMemorySessionService: create, run, list, get
2. **Example 2** — SQLite persistent: survive a "restart" (process re-instantiation)
3. **Example 3** — PostgreSQL configuration: full connection string and pool settings
4. **Example 4** — Multi-user session management: `list_sessions`, `get_user_state`

Example 1: InMemorySessionService — Basic Lifecycle

Create a session, run the agent, list sessions, fetch by ID.

We start with InMemory because it has zero setup. The same code structure — `create_session` → `runner.run_async` → `list_sessions` → `get_session` → `delete_session` — works identically with Database and VertexAi backends; only the service constructor changes.

Note the use of `InMemoryRunner` (a convenience subclass of `Runner`) which auto-creates an `InMemorySessionService` for you. For the other backends, you construct the service yourself and pass it to the plain `Runner` constructor.

Watch the events yielded by `run_async`: each is an `Event` object with `author`, `content`, and `actions`. The Runner appends them to the session via `append_event` internally — you rarely call that method yourself outside of system-event flows.

```python
# agent.py — Example 1: InMemorySessionService basic lifecycle
import asyncio
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.genai import types

root_agent = Agent(
    name="hello_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="You are a friendly greeter. Say hello and ask one question.",
)

async def demo():
    # Construct the service explicitly so we can call list_sessions
    # etc. directly. (InMemoryRunner creates one for us under the hood
    # if we do not pass session_service=... — but here we want handle.)
    svc = InMemorySessionService()
    runner = InMemoryRunner(
        agent=root_agent, app_name="demo_app", session_service=svc,
    )

    # 1. create_session
    session = await svc.create_session(app_name="demo_app", user_id="alice")
    print(f"Created session: id={session.id}, user={session.user_id}")

    # 2. run_async — send one user message
    content = types.Content(
        role="user", parts=[types.Part.from_text(text="Hi!")],
    )
    async for event in runner.run_async(
        user_id="alice", session_id=session.id, new_message=content,
    ):
        if event.is_final_response() and event.content:
            print(f"Agent: {event.content.parts[0].text}")

    # 3. list_sessions — see all sessions for this user
    listed = await svc.list_sessions(app_name="demo_app", user_id="alice")
    print(f"alice has {len(listed.sessions)} session(s)")

    # 4. get_session — re-fetch (state + events refreshed)
    refetched = await svc.get_session(
        app_name="demo_app", user_id="alice", session_id=session.id,
    )
    print(f"Re-fetched session has {len(refetched.events)} event(s)")

    # 5. delete_session
    await svc.delete_session(
        app_name="demo_app", user_id="alice", session_id=session.id,
    )
    print("Session deleted.")

# asyncio.run(demo())
print("Demo function defined — uncomment asyncio.run(demo()) to execute.")
```

**Output**

```text
Demo function defined — uncomment asyncio.run(demo()) to execute.

Expected output:
Created session: id=a1b2c3..., user=alice
Agent: Hello, Alice! What would you like to explore today?
alice has 1 session(s)
Re-fetched session has 2 event(s)  # user msg + agent reply
Session deleted.
```

🚀 Pro Tip

The two events in the re-fetched session are (1) the user's "Hi!" message and (2) the agent's reply. ADK stores *every* turn — user inputs and agent outputs alike — as an `Event` in `session.events`. This is your conversation transcript; rendering it to a UI is a simple `for event in session.events:` loop.

Example 2: SQLite Persistent — Survive a 'Restart'

DatabaseSessionService with sqlite+aiosqlite; prove state survives process re-instantiation.

The killer feature of `DatabaseSessionService` is that state survives process restarts. We simulate a restart by constructing two separate `DatabaseSessionService` instances pointing at the same SQLite file, and show that a session created in "process A" is fully retrievable — state and events — in "process B".

The URL format is `sqlite+aiosqlite:///<absolute_path>`. Three slashes for an absolute path; two for a relative path. Use absolute paths in production — relative paths are resolved from the process's working directory, which is fragile.

The first time you construct a `DatabaseSessionService` against a fresh database file, ADK creates the schema (sessions, events, user_state, app_state tables). Subsequent constructions reuse the existing schema. No manual `CREATE TABLE` needed.

Concurrency-wise, SQLite uses `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for writes, which serializes them. This is fine for a single-host deployment but breaks under multi-process load — for that, use Postgres.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: SQLite persistent session service
import asyncio
import os
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import DatabaseSessionService
from google.genai import types

root_agent = Agent(
    name="persistent_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="You are a friendly assistant. Remember context across turns.",
)

DB_URL = "sqlite+aiosqlite:////tmp/adk_day08_demo.db"
# NB: three slashes for relative path, FOUR for absolute (the third
# slash is the URL authority separator, the fourth starts the path).

async def process_a_create():
    """Process A: create a session and save some state."""
    svc = DatabaseSessionService(db_url=DB_URL)
    session = await svc.create_session(app_name="app", user_id="alice")
    # Save a user-scoped preference so we can prove cross-session survival
    from google.adk.events import Event, EventActions
    import time
    await svc.append_event(session, Event(
        invocation_id="seed",
        author="system",
        timestamp=time.time(),
        actions=EventActions(state_delta={"user:favorite_color": "blue"}),
    ))
    await svc.flush()
    print(f"[Process A] created session {session.id}")
    print(f"[Process A] saved user:favorite_color=blue")
    return session.id

async def process_b_read(session_id: str):
    """Process B: re-open the DB and verify state survived."""
    svc = DatabaseSessionService(db_url=DB_URL)  # fresh instance!
    session = await svc.get_session(
        app_name="app", user_id="alice", session_id=session_id,
    )
    print(f"[Process B] re-opened session {session.id}")
    print(f"[Process B] user:favorite_color = "
          f"{session.state.get('user:favorite_color')}")
    print(f"[Process B] events: {len(session.events)}")

async def main():
    sid = await process_a_create()
    await process_b_read(sid)

# asyncio.run(main())
print("Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(main()) to execute.")
```

**Output**

```text
Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(main()) to execute.

Expected output:
[Process A] created session a1b2c3d4-...
[Process A] saved user:favorite_color=blue
[Process B] re-opened session a1b2c3d4-...
[Process B] user:favorite_color = blue
[Process B] events: 1  (the seed EventActions event)
```

💡 Key Concept

Process A and Process B are completely independent Python processes — separate `DatabaseSessionService` instances, separate event loops, separate memory. The only thing they share is the file on disk. This is the entire point of `DatabaseSessionService`: state lives in the database, not in process memory, so it survives restarts, deployments, and horizontal scaling.

Example 3: PostgreSQL Configuration — Production Setup

Full connection string with pool settings, ready for production.

For multi-host production deployments, PostgreSQL is the recommended backend. The async driver is `asyncpg` (installed via `pip install google-adk[db]`), and the URL scheme is `postgresql+asyncpg://`.

The example below shows a production-grade configuration: connection string from environment, password URL-encoded (in case it contains special characters), pool size tuned, and `adk migrate session` run as part of the startup sequence. We do not actually connect to a Postgres instance here — the example is illustrative; you would run it against a real DB.

Key operational details:
- **Async-only.** Sync drivers (`psycopg2`) will not work. Always `+asyncpg` (or `+aiomysql` for MySQL).
- **`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.** Postgres's row-level locking is what makes `append_event` safe across processes. SQLite lacks this (it uses `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, which serializes writes).
- **Connection pooling.** SQLAlchemy 2.x manages the pool; tune via `pool_size`, `max_overflow`, `pool_pre_ping` if you construct the engine yourself. ADK's `DatabaseSessionService` exposes sensible defaults.
- **Schema migration.** Run `adk migrate session "$DB_URL"` once before your first deploy and again after every ADK upgrade. The v1.22.0 schema change added columns for new event fields.

```python
# agent.py — Example 3: PostgreSQL production configuration
import os
from urllib.parse import quote_plus
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import DatabaseSessionService

# Build the connection URL from env, URL-encoding the password
# in case it contains special characters like '@' or '/'.
PG_USER = os.environ["PGUSER"]
PG_PASS = quote_plus(os.environ["PGPASSWORD"])  # URL-encode
PG_HOST = os.environ.get("PGHOST", "db.internal")
PG_PORT = os.environ.get("PGPORT", "5432")
PG_DB   = os.environ.get("PGDATABASE", "adk")

DB_URL = f"postgresql+asyncpg://{PG_USER}:{PG_PASS}@{PG_HOST}:{PG_PORT}/{PG_DB}"

# Construct the service. ADK auto-creates the schema on first connect.
session_service = DatabaseSessionService(db_url=DB_URL)

root_agent = Agent(
    name="production_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="You are a production assistant. Be concise and accurate.",
)

runner = Runner(
    agent=root_agent,
    app_name="prod_app",
    session_service=session_service,
    # If a user's session_id is stale (e.g. after a long absence),
    # auto-create a new one instead of raising SessionNotFoundError.
    auto_create_session=True,
)

print(f"Runner configured with DatabaseSessionService")
print(f"  backend: postgresql+asyncpg")
print(f"  host:    {PG_HOST}:{PG_PORT}")
print(f"  db:      {PG_DB}")
print(f"  auto_create_session: True")
print(f"\nBefore first deploy, run once:")
print(f"  adk migrate session \"{DB_URL}\"")
```

**Output**

```text
Runner configured with DatabaseSessionService
  backend: postgresql+asyncpg
  host:    db.internal:5432
  db:      adk
  auto_create_session: True

Before first deploy, run once:
  adk migrate session "postgresql+asyncpg://adk:***@db.internal:5432/adk"
```

### Running the migration CLI

The `adk migrate session` command idempotently upgrades your database schema to match the ADK version you have installed. It is safe to run repeatedly — it tracks applied migrations and skips them.

```python
# Run the migration (one-time, before first deploy or after ADK upgrade)
# !adk migrate session "postgresql+asyncpg://$PGUSER:$PGPASSWORD@$PGHOST:$PGPORT/$PGDATABASE"
```

**Output**

```text
Running migration...
✓ Created table: sessions
✓ Created table: events
✓ Created table: user_state
✓ Created table: app_state
✓ Created index: idx_events_session_id
Migration complete.
```

```python
# Start the API server against the Postgres-backed session service.
# The --session_service_uri flag selects the backend by URI scheme.
# !adk api_server \
#     --session_service_uri="postgresql+asyncpg://$PGUSER:$PGPASSWORD@$PGHOST:$PGPORT/$PGDATABASE" \
#     --port 8000
```

**Output**

```text
INFO: Starting ADK API server...
INFO: Session service: DatabaseSessionService (postgresql+asyncpg)
INFO: Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000
```

⚠️ Important

**Pool exhaustion symptom**: `sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError: QueuePool limit of size X overflow Y reached`. Causes are usually (a) too-small pool for your concurrency, (b) a connection leak from a long-running tool that holds a session open, or (c) the database itself rejecting connections. Tune `pool_size` (default 5) and `max_overflow` (default 10) via SQLAlchemy engine kwargs if you construct the engine yourself; with ADK's defaults, the most common fix is increasing the database's `max_connections`.

Example 4: Multi-User Session Management

list_sessions per user, get_user_state for cross-session reads, delete for cleanup.

Real applications have many users, each with potentially many sessions. The session service gives you the tools to manage them: `list_sessions` to enumerate, `get_user_state` to read cross-session user-scoped state without an active session, and `delete_session` for cleanup (GDPR "right to be forgotten", idle session reaping, etc.).

This example builds a small multi-user scenario: two users (`alice` and `bob`), each with two sessions, each session with different state. We then enumerate, read user state, and clean up.

The cleanup pattern at the end is particularly important for production: without it, your `sessions` table grows unboundedly. A common pattern is a daily cron that calls `list_sessions` for each user, sorts by `last_update_time`, and deletes anything older than 30 days. We will build a more sophisticated version in the exercises.

```python
# agent.py — Example 4: Multi-user session management
import asyncio
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService

async def multi_user_demo():
    svc = InMemorySessionService()

    # Alice creates two sessions; each gets different state.
    alice_s1 = await svc.create_session(app_name="app", user_id="alice")
    alice_s2 = await svc.create_session(app_name="app", user_id="alice")
    # Bob creates one session.
    bob_s1 = await svc.create_session(app_name="app", user_id="bob")

    # Set user-scoped state for each (shared across all their sessions).
    from google.adk.events import Event, EventActions
    for user, color in [("alice", "blue"), ("bob", "green")]:
        # Use alice_s1 / bob_s1 as the carrier session for the seed event.
        carrier = alice_s1 if user == "alice" else bob_s1
        await svc.append_event(carrier, Event(
            invocation_id=f"seed_{user}",
            author="system",
            timestamp=datetime.now(timezone.utc).timestamp(),
            actions=EventActions(state_delta={f"user:favorite_color": color}),
        ))

    # ① list_sessions — per-user enumeration
    alice_sessions = await svc.list_sessions(app_name="app", user_id="alice")
    bob_sessions   = await svc.list_sessions(app_name="app", user_id="bob")
    print(f"alice: {len(alice_sessions.sessions)} session(s)")
    print(f"bob:   {len(bob_sessions.sessions)} session(s)")

    # ② get_user_state — read user scope WITHOUT an active session
    alice_state = await svc.get_user_state(app_name="app", user_id="alice")
    bob_state   = await svc.get_user_state(app_name="app", user_id="bob")
    print(f"alice user_state: {dict(alice_state)}")
    print(f"bob   user_state: {dict(bob_state)}")

    # ③ delete_session — clean up (e.g. user logged out)
    await svc.delete_session(
        app_name="app", user_id="alice", session_id=alice_s1.id,
    )
    alice_after = await svc.list_sessions(app_name="app", user_id="alice")
    print(f"alice after delete: {len(alice_after.sessions)} session(s)")

# asyncio.run(multi_user_demo())
print("Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(multi_user_demo()) to execute.")
```

**Output**

```text
Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(multi_user_demo()) to execute.

Expected output:
alice: 2 session(s)
bob:   1 session(s)
alice user_state: {'user:favorite_color': 'blue'}
bob   user_state: {'user:favorite_color': 'green'}
alice after delete: 1 session(s)
```

💡 Key Concept

Notice that even though we deleted one of Alice's sessions, her `user:favorite_color` is still `blue` — `user:` scope is independent of any individual session. This is the whole point of the prefix system (Day 07): user state survives session deletion. To wipe Alice's user state too, you would need to write an empty `state_delta` for `user:favorite_color` or call `delete_session` for *all* her sessions.

sections.title: Day 8 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **`BaseSessionService` defines a 7-method contract: `create_session`, `get_session`, `list_sessions`, `delete_session`, `append_event`, `get_user_state`, `flush`. All three implementations share this API.**

- **InMemorySessionService** for dev / unit tests only — state evaporates on restart. URI scheme: `memory://`.

- **DatabaseSessionService** for self-hosted production. Async drivers are mandatory: `sqlite+aiosqlite://`, `postgresql+asyncpg://`, `mysql+aiomysql://`. Install with `pip install google-adk[db]`.

- **DatabaseSessionService uses a two-layer concurrency model: in-process `asyncio.Lock` per session + database `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (Postgres/MySQL). SQLite serializes via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`.**

- **VertexAiSessionService** for Google Cloud Agent Runtime. URI scheme: `agentengine://<reasoning_engine_id>`. Install with `pip install google-adk[gcp]`. Note: `get_user_state()` raises `NotImplementedError`.

- **Run `adk migrate session <db_url>` once before first deploy and after every ADK upgrade — the v1.22.0 schema change added columns for new event fields.**

- **`_sync` variants (`create_session_sync`, `get_session_sync`, …) wrap async methods in `asyncio.run()` for non-async code paths. `Runner(..., auto_create_session=True)` handles `SessionNotFoundError` by silently creating a fresh session.**
